Q004655:
## What an AIP Logic function is
AIP Logic is Palantir's no-code way to build an LLM-powered function. It has typed inputs and outputs, a system prompt and a task prompt with injected variables, and blocks that can call tools, branch or loop. A function can also make Ontology edits, so its output changes real objects.
## Why versions and traces matter
Applications and automations call a **published version**. Each run leaves an execution trace: the exact prompt after variables were injected, every tool call and its result, the raw model output and the edit that was applied. When behaviour changes right after an edit, the trace shows which stage changed instead of leaving you to guess.
- Classify the failure first: prompt design, block wiring, tool configuration, model behaviour or execution logic.
- Protect consumers: they should stay on the last known-good version while you debug.
- Example: if the new prompt says "flag anything mentioning pressure as urgent", the trace will show that sentence driving the urgent output on routine pressure checks.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Larger model:** a stronger model still follows the edited prompt, so a prompt that now asks for the wrong thing keeps producing the wrong priority. It adds cost without finding the cause.
- ✗ **B. Rewrite in code:** AIP Logic runs can be debugged through their traces and earlier versions stay available. Rewriting in code throws away working logic and still does not explain what the prompt edit broke.
- ✗ **C. Higher temperature:** temperature adds randomness to the output; it does not fix a changed instruction and makes priorities less consistent. Publishing at once also pushes an untested change to every consumer.
- ✓ **D. Trace comparison with a known-good version (correct):** the problem appeared right after a prompt change, so the trace of a failing ticket against the previous version locates the stage that broke. Keeping consumers on that version stops wrong priorities reaching the Ontology while the fix is tested.

## Key idea
When an AI function changes behaviour, read the trace against the last good version and keep consumers on that version until the fix is proven.
Q004656:
## What the agent has to get right
An AIP agent combines a model, instructions, retrieval context and tools. This one can do two kinds of things: answer from manuals (read) and create a work order (write). The write tool is where a mistake has real consequences.
## A release test set
The exam guide asks for testing with representative, edge and adversarial interactions before release. A practical set for this agent:
- Typical: common fault questions the manuals cover.
- Edge: a model not in the manuals, two manuals that disagree, a question with missing information.
- Insufficient evidence: the agent should say it cannot find support, not invent a procedure.
- Write path: a request missing required fields, a user without permission to create work orders, an instruction hidden inside a pasted log.
Run these before launch and keep them as a regression suite for every later change.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Prompt instruction:** a sentence in the prompt cannot guarantee behaviour and gives no evidence of quality. Controls on the tool and a tested refusal path do; the prompt is not a test.
- ✗ **B. Use production as the test:** users would meet unsafe answers and wrong work orders first. Production feedback is valuable for improving the suite, but it does not replace testing before release.
- ✓ **C. Typical, edge and adversarial cases (correct):** a demo only shows the happy path. Production failures come from unanswerable questions, conflicting sources and misuse of the write tool, so those cases must be tested before technicians rely on the agent.
- ✗ **D. Rephrased demo questions:** this measures consistency on easy questions only. It never checks what the agent does when evidence is missing or when the work order tool is misused.

## Key idea
Before releasing an agent, test typical, edge, insufficient-evidence and adversarial cases, with extra focus on tools that change data.
Q004657:
## How semantic search works
An embedding model turns text into a vector, a list of numbers that places similar meanings close together. At indexing time every chunk is embedded and stored, for example as a vector property on an object. At query time the question is embedded and the nearest chunk vectors are returned.
## Why the model must match
Each embedding model builds its own vector space. Distances are only meaningful between vectors from the same model, so a query vector from model B compared with chunk vectors from model A gives nearly random neighbours.
- The exam guide states the rule directly: use the same embedding model for indexing and query-time retrieval.
- Example: "parental leave eligibility" embedded with the new model may land closest to an expense policy chunk embedded with the old one.
When you upgrade the model, re-embed the corpus, rebuild the index, then switch queries, and compare retrieval quality on an evaluation set before and after.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. Mismatched embedding models (correct):** query and chunk vectors from different models are not comparable, which explains a sudden drop right after the switch. Re-embedding the corpus (or reverting the query model) puts both sides back in one vector space.
- ✗ **B. Prompt filtering:** the problem is in retrieval, before the model sees anything. A prompt cannot make the right chunk appear when the search never returns it.
- ✗ **C. Bigger chunks:** chunk size affects precision and context, but it did not change here. The drop began when only the query model changed, and larger chunks would still be compared across two vector spaces.
- ✗ **D. More chunks:** retrieving more neighbours from a broken similarity ranking adds more unrelated text. It raises token use and noise without restoring relevance.

## Key idea
Embed queries and documents with the same model; after a model change, re-embed the corpus before switching queries.
Q004658:
## South or north of the Ontology
Palantir describes the Ontology as the semantic layer between data pipelines and applications. Work **south** of it runs in pipelines and publishes data into object properties. Work **north** of it runs at interaction time, in functions, agents and apps.
## Choosing the layer
The exam guide asks you to justify the layer with consumer breadth, freshness, reusability, scale and cost.
- South: many consumers need the same result, the input is large, a nightly refresh is fresh enough. Compute once, validate, store, reuse.
- North: the reasoning depends on the user's current context or question, so it cannot be computed ahead of time.
- Auditability: for batch enrichment, keep the prompt and the raw response next to the parsed output so wrong labels can be traced and reprocessed.
Example: a category used for filtering by five apps is computed once per ticket in the pipeline; "draft a reply to this customer given what I just wrote" belongs north.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Generate on view:** every view repeats the same LLM call, so cost grows with traffic, the label is missing for filters and dashboards that never open the ticket, and two views can return different labels.
- ✓ **B. Batch step in the pipeline (correct):** one reusable label per ticket, needed by many consumers, at large scale and nightly freshness, is exactly the case for south-of-Ontology processing. Structured output and validation keep the property usable for filtering, and stored prompts and responses support audits.
- ✗ **C. Classify inside the agent:** labels would exist only inside conversations. Other apps could not filter on them, and 2 million tickets cannot be processed through chat sessions.
- ✗ **D. One function per app:** each team gets different labels for the same ticket, the work is repeated for every app, and nothing is validated or stored for audit.

## Key idea
Reusable, large-scale enrichment that many consumers need runs south of the Ontology; context-dependent reasoning for one user runs north.
Q004659:
## Why one run is not enough
Model outputs are non-deterministic: the same input can produce a different answer on another run. On 50 cases, one case is 2 points, so a 3-point gap can be just one or two cases flipping by chance.
## Separating three explanations
The exam guide asks you to tell apart a real regression, expected variance and a change in the test distribution.
- Variance: run each version several times on the same suite and look at the spread of scores.
- Regression: the candidate fails the same cases consistently, ideally cases of one kind (for example, every multi-step calculation).
- Distribution change: confirm the suite, evaluators and target function were identical for both runs.
Example: if the current model scores 87-92% over five runs and the candidate 86-90%, the gap is inside the noise; if the candidate always fails the four unit-conversion cases, that is a real regression in one area.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Revert on any drop:** a single-run difference of one or two cases can be noise. Reverting without evidence may discard a better model.
- ✗ **B. New self-graded suite:** changing the test set at the same time as the model makes the two scores incomparable, and letting the candidate grade its own answers biases the result.
- ✓ **C. Repeated runs and case inspection (correct):** measuring run-to-run spread shows whether 3 points is signal, and looking at which cases change shows whether the failures are systematic. Holding the suite fixed rules out a distribution change.
- ✗ **D. Five-point rule:** no fixed threshold separates noise from regression; it depends on suite size and variance. A consistent failure on a small group of cases can be a real regression even at 3 points.

## Key idea
Before calling a regression, measure variance with repeated runs on a fixed suite and inspect which cases change.
Q004660:
## Where duplicates come from
Automate runs effects when a trigger fires, and it can retry when a step fails or times out. A timeout does not always mean the work failed: the Action may have finished after the caller stopped waiting. A retry then runs the whole chain again and creates a second record.
## Idempotent writes
An operation is idempotent when running it twice has the same effect as running it once.
- Give the write a natural key, here the invoice: one invoice, at most one payment request.
- Check for an existing request (or a stored operation status) before creating one; if it exists, return it instead of creating another.
- Keep retries: they recover from genuine temporary failures, which is why you make the write safe rather than removing them.
The exam guide asks for workflows that stay safe when an AI call, Action or external dependency fails or is retried.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Disable retries:** genuine temporary failures would leave invoices unprocessed, and a manual weekly catch-up delays payments. The real defect, an unsafe write, stays in place.
- ✗ **B. Prompt instruction:** the extraction model does not create the payment request; the Action does. A prompt cannot enforce a data constraint at the write boundary.
- ✗ **C. Longer timeout:** timeouts and retries can still happen for other reasons, such as an overloaded dependency, and every retry would still create a duplicate.
- ✓ **D. Idempotent Action (correct):** keying the payment request to the invoice and checking before creating makes every retry harmless, so temporary failures are still recovered without duplicate payments.

## Key idea
When a workflow retries, make every write idempotent so a repeated run cannot duplicate its effect.
Q004661:
## Reading a trace for latency
A trace lists each step with its duration. Here two things dominate:
- Three independent retrieval calls run one after another, so their times add up. Independent steps can run in parallel.
- A 60,000-token prompt: model latency and cost grow with input tokens, and low-relevance chunks add noise that can lower answer quality.
## Targeted optimization
The exam guide asks you to profile the trace and recommend a targeted optimization rather than simply choosing a larger model. Typical levers are fewer or parallel calls, smaller and more relevant context, caching where safe, and asynchronous execution for genuinely long work. After any change, run the regression evaluation to confirm quality, safety and cost did not get worse.
Example: tightening retrieval to the top relevant chunks could cut the context to around 8,000 tokens, and parallel retrieval removes two sequential waits.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Nightly batch:** users ask new questions interactively; precomputed answers cannot respond to them. Asynchronous work suits long jobs, not a few-second assistant.
- ✓ **B. Parallel retrieval and smaller context (correct):** these are the two bottlenecks the trace shows. Both reduce latency directly, and trimming irrelevant chunks often improves grounding too; the evaluation run checks that quality holds.
- ✗ **C. Larger model:** larger models are usually slower and more expensive per token. It does nothing about the sequential retrievals or the oversized context.
- ✗ **D. More capacity:** the trace shows workflow structure and prompt size as the cost, not queuing at the provider. Capacity would not shorten sequential calls or a 60,000-token input.

## Key idea
Profile the trace first: parallelize independent steps and cut irrelevant context before reaching for a bigger model.
Q004662:
## What prompt injection is
Prompt injection hides instructions inside data the model reads, here an email. A model cannot reliably tell the user's instructions from text inside the content it was asked to process, so any tool it holds can be triggered by an attacker who controls that content.
## Enforce controls outside the prompt
The exam guide is explicit: do not rely on prompts to enforce policy; enforce least privilege at the data, retrieval, tool, Action and execution boundaries, and add human review for high-consequence actions.
- Least privilege: a summarizer needs to read, not write. Remove the write tool from this agent.
- Separate recommend from execute: the agent may suggest a change; an Action with validation (allowed ranges, required fields) performs it.
- Human review: credit limits are high-consequence, so a person approves.
With these in place, a successful injection can at most produce a misleading summary, not a financial change.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. Read-only agent and an approved Action (correct):** taking the write tool away removes what the attacker wants to trigger, and the separate Action enforces validation and approval at the boundary where the change happens.
- ✗ **B. Prompt rule:** instructions in the prompt can be overridden or confused by injected text; they reduce risk at best and cannot be the main control for a financial write.
- ✗ **C. Log and reverse later:** auditing detects damage after it happened. The unauthorized credit-limit change still takes effect and may be used before anyone reverses it.
- ✗ **D. Phrase blocklist:** attackers can reword the instruction in endless ways. Keyword filters miss variants and give a false sense of safety.

## Key idea
Treat content as untrusted: limit tools to what the task needs, and put validation and human approval on high-consequence Actions.
Q004671:
## Typed inputs and outputs in AIP Logic
AIP Logic functions declare their inputs and outputs with types: strings, numbers, booleans, enumerations, lists, object references and structs. The output type is part of the function's contract: whatever consumes the function receives that shape, not whatever the model happened to write.
## Why this matters for automations
An automation or a Workshop app cannot negotiate with prose. When the output is typed, a priority that is not one of the three allowed values fails inside the function, where it can be retried or surfaced, rather than breaking the consumer later.
- Enumerated output: the priority can only be low, medium or high.
- Numeric output: the confidence is a number, not "about 80%".
- The consumer reads fields, so a wording change in the model's reasoning cannot break it.
Example: output `{priority: high, confidence: 0.82}` works for every consumer; the sentence "I would rate this as High (82%)" works only until the model phrases it differently.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Lower temperature:** less randomness makes the format more consistent but does not guarantee it; the consumer still parses prose and still breaks on any variation.
- ✗ **B. JSON in the prompt:** asking for JSON in prose still leaves the model free to add text or malformed JSON, and the consumer still carries the parsing and validation burden.
- ✗ **C. Regular expression:** pattern matching on free text is brittle; a sentence such as "not high priority, confidence low" produces the wrong priority and the wrong number.
- ✓ **D. Typed structured output (correct):** the contract moves from "parse whatever the model says" to "the function returns this structure", which removes the format drift that causes the failures.

## Key idea
Give an AIP Logic function a typed output; consumers should receive a structure, not text to parse.
Q004672:
## Single completion versus tool-using reasoning
AIP Logic offers two ways to use the model:
- A **single completion** sends one prompt with the injected inputs and takes the answer. It is fast, cheap and predictable.
- A **tool-using reasoning** block lets the model decide, over several steps, which tools to call (Ontology queries, functions, other Logic) before answering. It is for tasks where the needed information is not in the inputs.
## Matching the block to the task
The exam guide asks you to choose single completion or tool-using reasoning appropriately. Summarizing text that is already an input needs no lookup. Giving the model tools anyway adds latency per step, cost per call, and a new failure mode: calling tools it does not need and pulling unrelated data into the answer.
Example: "summarize this transcript" is a completion; "summarize this transcript and link each action item to the owner's open tasks" would justify tools.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. More iterations:** this lets the model make even more tool calls, so runs get longer and the chance of unrelated data in the summary rises.
- ✓ **B. Single completion without tools (correct):** the transcript is already an input, so the model has everything it needs. Removing the tools removes the slow steps and the irrelevant lookups at the same time.
- ✗ **C. More tools:** the function would gain more ways to fetch data the task does not need; the problem is that tools are present at all, not that two are missing.
- ✗ **D. Larger model:** a stronger model may pick tools more sensibly but is slower and dearer, and it still cannot make an unnecessary lookup useful.

## Key idea
Use tool-using reasoning only when the answer needs data that is not in the inputs; otherwise a single completion is faster, cheaper and more predictable.
Q004673:
## Deterministic logic or AI
The exam guide's first decision area is whether a task is a fixed, reproducible rule or needs interpretation. "Amount greater than 10,000" is a rule. Letting a language model apply it means accepting a small error rate on something that never needed judgement.
## Blocks in AIP Logic
A Logic function is a sequence of blocks: completions, tool calls, conditionals, loops and edits. A **conditional** branches on a typed input or on an earlier block's output. Here the amount is a typed number, so the branch is evaluated exactly, and the model only does the part that needs language: writing the note in the chosen template.
This also makes the function easier to test: each branch can be checked with a claim on either side of the threshold.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. Conditional block on the amount (correct):** the threshold becomes deterministic code inside the function, and the model is only asked to write text within the template that the branch selected.
- ✗ **B. Run twice:** this doubles cost and latency and still relies on the model to apply the rule; two guesses are not a guarantee.
- ✗ **C. Threshold tool:** fetching the rule from a tool makes it configurable, but the comparison is still performed by the model rather than by code.
- ✗ **D. Emphasize the rule in the prompt:** the rule stays a request to the model, so it can still be missed; prompt emphasis reduces errors but does not remove them.

## Key idea
Put fixed rules in conditional blocks; reserve the model for the parts that need language or interpretation.
Q004674:
## Applying Ontology edits safely
An Ontology edit from a Logic function changes real objects that people and automations rely on. The exam guide asks you to apply Ontology edits safely: an edit should depend on the object's current state, not only on the incoming evidence.
## Allowed transitions
Order statuses usually form a state machine: New → Shipped → Delivered, with Cancelled as a terminal state. "Cancelled → Shipped" is not a valid transition no matter what an email says. A conditional block can read the current status before the edit block runs:
- allowed transition: apply the edit;
- not allowed: skip the edit and flag the order so a person can check whether the cancellation or the shipment is wrong.
Example: an email for order 1182 (status Cancelled) is logged as "shipment reported for cancelled order", not written as Shipped.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Daily batch:** a cancellation can still happen after the daily run, and delaying every status update by a day harms the normal case without fixing the conflict.
- ✗ **B. Append to notes:** this avoids the overwrite but stops the function from doing its job for the normal case, so every shipment would need a manual status update.
- ✓ **C. Precondition on current status (correct):** the edit is only applied for valid transitions and conflicting evidence is routed to review, which is exactly the "edit safely" pattern.
- ✗ **D. Prompt instruction:** the model does not see the current status unless the function provides it, and a prompt rule can be misapplied; the guard belongs in logic that reads the object.

## Key idea
Before an Ontology edit, read the object's current state and only apply transitions that are allowed; send conflicts to review.
Q004675:
## When code is more suitable than AIP Logic
The exam guide asks you to understand when code is more suitable than AIP Logic. AIP Logic is for tasks that need language understanding or flexible interpretation. Three signals point to code here:
- **Determinism**: currency conversion with fixed rounding rules has exactly one correct answer per input.
- **Scale**: two million rows per night is a pipeline-scale batch, where per-row model calls would be slow and expensive.
- **Scheduling and control**: a nightly job with rate limits and programmatic control is what Code Repositories are for.
A language model is not a calculator: even at temperature zero it can produce wrong arithmetic, and it cannot be audited the way a rounding function can.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. Code in a repository (correct):** deterministic arithmetic at batch scale on a schedule is the textbook case for a transform or function, giving exact results, testability and low cost.
- ✗ **B. Loop block:** looping two million completions through a Logic function is slow and expensive and still trusts the model with exact arithmetic.
- ✗ **C. Agent with calculator:** an agent adds reasoning, latency and cost to a task with no judgement in it, and the calculator tool does the only part that matters.
- ✗ **D. Logic with temperature zero:** zero temperature makes output more repeatable, not correct; model arithmetic and rounding errors remain, and two million completions a night are costly.

## Key idea
Deterministic, large-scale, scheduled computation belongs in code; AIP Logic is for tasks that need language or interpretation.
Q004676:
## Tuning parameters
AIP Logic exposes model parameters such as temperature and maximum output tokens. **Temperature** controls randomness: higher values let the model pick less likely tokens, which helps creative writing and hurts classification. A classifier should be as deterministic as possible, so a low temperature is the first setting to change.
## Constrain the output type
A typed enumerated output removes a second source of variation: the model cannot answer "mostly shipping, maybe billing" when the contract is one of six values. Together, low temperature and an enumeration make repeated runs far more consistent.
After tuning, rerun the evaluation suite several times; the remaining spread tells you how much variance is still inherent to the model, which matters when you judge future changes.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. More retrieved context:** a classifier of review text needs no retrieval; extra context adds noise and makes behaviour depend on which neighbours were returned.
- ✗ **B. Three runs, keep the last:** the last answer is no more reliable than the first, and three completions triple the cost without reducing randomness.
- ✓ **C. Low temperature plus enumerated output (correct):** the two settings target the two causes of run-to-run variation, randomness in generation and freedom in the output format.
- ✗ **D. More output tokens:** longer explanations do not make the final label more stable; they add cost and give the model more room to wander.

## Key idea
For classification, lower the temperature and constrain the output to the allowed values before changing anything else.
Q004677:
## Versions in AIP Logic
A Logic function is edited as a draft and released by **publishing** a version. Consumers (Workshop, Automate, other functions) use a published version, so editing and publishing are separate steps. The exam guide asks engineers to publish versions and preserve behaviour for existing consumers.
## A safe release
- Make the change in the draft and run the evaluation suite against it.
- Publish it as a new version; the earlier version keeps serving current consumers.
- Update the consumers one by one, checking each; if something breaks, that consumer goes back to the earlier version.
This is the same discipline as software releases: new behaviour ships behind a version boundary, and rollback is a configuration change, not an emergency edit.
Example: the new output field is added in version 4; the Workshop app moves first, the two automations the following week after their owners confirm the new field.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Point consumers at a draft:** drafts change while being edited; consumers would follow every keystroke, which is the opposite of preserving behaviour.
- ✗ **B. New function and delete the old:** this duplicates the function's identity, breaks every reference to the old name on deletion and loses the version history.
- ✗ **C. Edit in place:** every consumer would receive untested behaviour at once, and there is no version to fall back to if the reworded prompt changes results.
- ✓ **D. New version, evaluate, migrate consumers (correct):** the previous version keeps working while the change is tested, and each consumer is switched only when its owner is ready.

## Key idea
Publish changes as a new version, evaluate, then migrate consumers deliberately while the old version stays available.
Q004678:
## Loops over typed lists
AIP Logic blocks include **loops**, which run a set of blocks once for each element of a list input or of an earlier block's output. Each iteration gets its own completion with just that element injected into the prompt, and the results are collected.
## Why one giant prompt fails
Putting hundreds of items into one prompt hits token limits, raises cost, and makes quality drop as the model's attention is spread across the whole list. Per-item completions are bounded in size regardless of the order, and a single bad item does not spoil the notes for the others.
Example: an order with 380 lines becomes 380 short completions, each with the same template and one item injected, returning a list of 380 notes in the same order.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Recursion on failure:** retrying halves after failures is unpredictable, wastes the failed attempts and is not a supported design for a Logic function.
- ✓ **B. Loop block per item (correct):** it fits the data shape (a list of independent items), keeps every prompt small and produces a typed list output the consumer can use.
- ✗ **C. Split orders upstream:** changing the data model to work around a function design corrupts the order's identity and still does not bound the prompt for a mid-sized order.
- ✗ **D. Maximum context:** larger context raises cost and latency and only postpones the limit; quality on very long prompts still degrades.

## Key idea
Process a list of independent items with a loop block, one bounded completion per item.
